claude.sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries (30 EHR documents x 6 LLMs)

links.outcome: Ability of automatic metrics and LLM judges to detect hallucinations in LLM summaries
links.effect: Both LLM judges identified only two of nine hallucinations detected by experts; metric correlations with expert hallucination scores were 0.10-0.23 (Spearman).
links.quote: However, both LLMs identified only two of the nine hallucinations detected by the experts.

links.outcome: Whether automated (metric/LLM-judge) comparison with expert review reliably estimates real-world summary accuracy
links.effect: Automatic metrics and LLM judges correlated only weakly to moderately with expert scores (e.g., BERTScore relevance 0.57; hallucinations 0.10-0.23); not reliable standalone evaluators.
links.quote: Therefore, biased assessments, preference for redundancy at the expense of accuracy, overestimation of the decision quality, and similar issues [ 24 ] prevent LLM judges from being considered reliable, autonomous evaluation tools, especially in the highly sensitive medical field.

links.outcome: Hallucinations and factual errors in LLM-generated EHR summaries (including numerical errors)
links.effect: Expert hallucination scores ranged 3.4-4.6 of 5 across models; examples included fabricated alcohol abuse and temperature 39.0 °C instead of 36.6 °C, the latter missed by the LLM judge.
links.quote: Consequently, the LLM-as-a-judge failed to detect a significant error where the reported body temperature was inaccurately stated as 39.0 °C instead of the correct 36.6 °C.

unlisted_practices: Using LLM-as-a-judge and automatic metrics (BERTScore, ROUGE) for automated quality evaluation of summaries
Using a judge model from a different family to avoid self-preference bias

links.effect: Experts detected 9 hallucinations; both LLM judges identified only 2 of 9.
links.quote: However, both LLMs identified only two of the nine hallucinations detected by the experts.

links.effect: Hallucinations Spearman coefficients were ROUGE-1 0.17, ROUGE-2 0.10, ROUGE-L 0.19, BLEU 0.11, METEOR 0.14, BERTScore 0.23.
links.quote: The expectedly low correlation between the automatic evaluation metrics and the expert scores provides evidence of their infeasibility as reliable independent evaluators.

links.effect: LLM-as-a-judge missed body temperature stated as 39.0 °C instead of 36.6 °C.
links.quote: Consequently, the LLM-as-a-judge failed to detect a significant error where the reported body temperature was inaccurately stated as 39.0 °C instead of the correct 36.6 °C.

unlisted_practices: Using off-the-shelf low-parameter LLM-as-a-judge plus automatic text-similarity metrics as a standalone quality-control system for medical text summaries

links.outcome: factual inaccuracies and hallucinations in LLM-generated summaries
links.effect: Experts detected 9 hallucinations across 180 summaries from 6 LLMs, including fabricated history, contradictory statements, and numerical analysis errors (reporting 39.0 °C instead of 36.6 °C).
links.quote: The analysis revealed several factual inaccuracies in LLM-generated summaries.

unlisted_practices: Automated evaluation of clinical text summaries using standard automatic NLP metrics and LLM-as-a-judge approaches without expert involvement

screen.practice: automated quality control of LLM summaries (LLM-as-a-judge and automatic metrics) versus expert review
screen.reason: The study empirically tests whether an automated safeguard practice (LLM-as-a-judge and automated metrics for quality control and hallucination detection) can reliably validate clinical summaries compared to human expert review.

primary.practice: LLM-as-a-judge automated quality and hallucination filtering
